narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence, and it worked in your favor by pulling the prediction toward passing. Unfortunately, two other factors pushed strongly in the opposite direction and outweighed that benefit. Your class ranking at the end of your first year and your class ranking at the end of your third year both signaled higher risk of bar exam failure. Both rankings placed you in the third decile, noticeably below the average of accepted students (around the sixth and fifth deciles respectively). These lower academic standings relative to your peers were the main reasons the model concluded you were more likely to struggle with the bar exam.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Retaking the LSAT to raise your score, improving your study habits to move higher in your class rankings, or enrolling in a strong bar-preparation program could meaningfully change your profile. Many students in similar situations have successfully improved their outcomes by targeting exactly these gaps before reapplying.
